coach_says: You're already two pawns down, and Nh5+ is about as good as anything here. The thing to keep an eye on is the white knight on d5: it hits e7 and threatens Nc7, forking your rooks on a8 and e8. Swapping it off with Nxd5+ is the simplest way to get rid of it, but Nh5+ is fine.
also: trade off the strong d5 knight

coach_says: Good. Kxc8 takes back the knight that just grabbed your bishop, and it is the engine's top choice. You're still behind, so now get your queenside pieces out (Nd7, and a rook to the f- or e-file) and look for active play against e5.

You were in trouble whatever you played: your knight on h4 is attacked by the queen on d8, and Black's bishop on b1 is attacked by your rook. You can save one of them, not both, so you're a piece down either way. Nf3 is fine; Bb5, pinning the c6 knight before you take back on b1, gets your pieces out a bit faster, but the difference is small.

White's bishop on d8 is lost in your camp: if c7 is defended, its only way home is back along e7-f6-g5. Be7 offers to trade it off and lets White off the hook (Bxe7 Nxe7). Bd6 defends c7 and keeps that bishop stuck: if White doesn't retreat at once, ...f6 or ...h6 traps it. When an enemy piece is offside and short of squares, don't trade it. Take its squares away.
also: don't swap off a bad enemy piece

coach_says: In rook endgames your king should be your most active piece. Kf4 heads straight for e3, next to White's king, where it helps your rook and your pawns. Kf5 is a step slower. After b4 hits your rook, your king is too far away to help, and White's rook on a5 gets active against your queenside pawns. Next time, walk your king toward the action.

Your knight on g3 was hanging: both the f2 pawn and the bishop on f4 attack it, and nothing defends it. g5 attacks the bishop, but White just plays Bxg3 and the bishop gets away by taking your knight. A counter-attack only works if the opponent can't simply take your loose piece first. Save the knight with Nf5 and you stay a piece up.

Your king on h6 is in a mating net: White threatened Ng4+, and that ends in mate. Kg7 doesn't fix it, because Nh5+ just drives the king back and Bc1+ follows. Rf8 was the defence. It attacks the f6 knight a second time and pins it to the queen on f3, so if the knight moves (Ng4+ or Nh5+), ...Rxf3 wins White's queen. When your king is under fire, look for a move that stops the attacking piece from moving.
also: king walking into a mating net

coach_says: Black's queen on d3 was attacking your rook on f1, and nothing defended it. Qf3 doesn't help, because your own f2 pawn blocks the queen from guarding f1, so ...Qxf1+ wins a whole rook. Before every move, ask what your opponent's last move attacks. Re1, Rd1 or Rh1 moves the rook to safety and you stay clearly better.
concept: missed the attack on the f1 rook

coach_says: Your b3 pawn was attacked twice, by the queen on b5 with the rook on b8 behind it, and defended only once. Ba7 attacks the rook, but Black just plays ...Qxb3, which guards b8 and hits your rook on a2 and your queen. Count attackers and defenders on your loose pawns before you start an attack of your own. Qc2 guards b3 and hits c7 at the same time.
concept: b3 pawn under a queen-rook battery

coach_says: Your king's cover is gone and the g-file is wide open. Bg5 puts your bishop right on that file in front of your king, so Rg1 pins it, and after ...Kh8 Bxg5 White wins it because it is attacked three times. When the file in front of your king is open, don't put a piece on it that can be pinned. Kh8 first, then ...Rg8, fights for the file.

Your king is still on e1, and the bishop on f1 stops it from stepping to f1. Black threatened ...Qb4+, checking and then grabbing e4 and your h1 rook (Qb4+ Rd2 Qb1+ Rd1 Qxe4+). c4 does nothing about that. Get the bishop out first (Bb5, Be2 or Bg2), so that after ...Qb4+ your king can go to f1 and is safe.

Black's queen on g6 was eyeing g2, and your bishop on f1 was its only defender. Bd3 attacks the queen, but it takes the defender away: ...Qxg2 gets out with a pawn and hits your rook on h1. Before you move a piece, check what it was guarding. Bg3 or Nf3 keeps everything defended.

White was already threatening your e5 pawn: after fxe5 dxe5, the bishop on c3 takes on e5. a4 attacks the b3 bishop, but White just swaps it off with Bxe6 and then wins e5 anyway. Before you chase a piece, check whether your opponent has a threat of their own. Bxb3 first, or a move that keeps e5 defended, holds the balance.

d5 opens the centre while your king is still on e8 and your kingside pieces are undeveloped. After exd5 exd5, White's bishop on c4, the knights and a queen on f3 all hit d5 and f7, and Re1+ comes down the open e-file. White wins a pawn with a strong attack. Finish developing and castle first (Be7 and O-O), then think about ...d5.

Black threatened mate: the queen on g5 and the knight on e3 both hit g2, and ...Qxg2 is mate. h4 doesn't stop it. Every move, look at every check your opponent has, especially against the squares around your king. g3, Kf2 or Bf1 would have stopped the mate.

Your king is still on e1 with Black's rook on the open e-file and their knight on e4. cxd5 lets Black start checking: ...Qb4+ Ke2 Nc5+ is a discovered check from the rook and mates soon after. With your king this exposed, check first. Qd4+ forces ...f6 and brings your queen back to defend.

White's knight on h6 threatened Nf7, and that is mate: your king on h8 can't go to g8 or g7 because of the queen on g3, and your own knight blocks h7. a5 ignores it. When your king is boxed in, check every knight jump near it. Qh5 guards f7 and you stay better.
also: king boxed in by its own pieces

coach_says: Bxc7 wins a pawn, but Qxb7 first was stronger, because it takes a pawn and attacks the rook on a8. Black has to save the rook, and c7 is still there to take next move. If you have two captures, start with the one that makes a threat, so your opponent never gets time to organise a defence.

With rook against rook and two pawns, your king's job is to stand in front of the pawns. Kg4 walks into ...h5+: the pawn checks your king away from the g- and h-pawns (it can't take on h5, because g6 guards it). Kg2 or Kh2 keeps your king in front of them, and Rxh7 comes next, so the game is a draw.
concept: king in front of enemy pawns

coach_says: Your knight on b5 was attacked by the queen on a6, and Nxc7 saves it with a fork: from c7 it hits both the queen on a6 and the rook on a8, so you win the rook and get your material back. Qb3+ lets Black block with ...Qe6 and offer a queen trade, and the fork is gone. When a piece is attacked, look for a square where it attacks two things.
